newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Singapore's UOB to merge its two Malaysian banks.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's UOB to merge its two Malaysian banks.

text.p: Singapore's United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB) announced plans on Thursday to merge its two Malaysian bank units, a move which will create Malaysia's 11th largest banking group.

The planned merger of Chung Khiaw Bank (M) Bhd and United Overseas Bank (M) Bhd would have combined assets of 10.3 billion ringgit ($4.12 billion), shareholders' funds of 839 million ringgit and 25 branches, UOB said in a statement.
"We had a choice of listing one of the two banks on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) to take immediate profit," said Wee Cho Yaw, chairman and chief executive officer of UOB.

"... We have decided to merge our two banks to demonstrate our long-term commitment to, and confidence, in Malaysia," Wee said at a news briefing in Kuala Lumpur. The merger was expected to be completed by the first quarter of 1997.
Chung Khiaw is the 16th largest bank among 37 commercial banks in Malaysia in terms of assets, while United Overseas Bank Malaysia was the 22nd largest bank, as at December 31, 1995.
After the merger, United Overseas Bank Malaysia would be the 11th largest bank in terms of assets, loans and deposits, UOB officials said.
Wee said the merged entity would retain the name of United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, and would be 100 percent controlled by its Singapore parent, as were the two units.

The move comes hot on the heels of the merger between DCB Holdings Bhd's DCB Bank and Kwong Yik Bank Bhd in November and the announcement by Sime Darby Bhd that it was looking to acquire a majority stake in Oriental Bank Bhd.
The rationalisation of Malaysian banks follows the government's urging to create greater economies of scale within the industry.
Malaysian banking rules allow for foreign-owned banks to exist in the country, but they are not allowed to open new branches.

The UOB statement said the bank was also starting a joint venture stockbroking firm with Affin Holdings Bhd Financial services firm Affin had said previously it would have a 55 percent equity interest in the planned joint venture.
Wee added that operations of the stockbroking venture could start in three to four months. "It depends on Affin," he said.
The merged banking entity would qualify as a Tier-1 bank under Malaysia's two-tier banking system, the statement said.
Tier-1 banks are allowed a more liberal operating environment and need to have a minimum of 640 million ringgit in shareholders' funds, as at December 31, 1996.
In 1997, the minimum requirement, set by Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, will go up to 820 million.
"The Tier-1 status puts it in a strong position. It gives it more flexibility than non Tier-1 local banks," said Teoh Kok Lin, head of research at brokers HSBC James Capel in Kuala Lumpur.
"Over time, they will be able to take market share away from non Tier-1 local banks," he said.
"But the fact that it is owned by a foreign bank means that it won't be able to expand its branch network," said another banking analyst at a local equities research house.
